content_html:
Continuity > Boundary > Update

Memory is neither a continuous recording nor a set of isolated snapshots. It is organised by three interacting operations: continuity binds neighbouring moments into a drifting context; boundary marks a prediction-error shift that separates one event from another; and update revises or creates schemas so that future experience can be encoded more efficiently.

Memory is often imagined as a storehouse: experience enters, is kept somewhere, and is later retrieved. A more useful model treats memory as an active organisation of experience over time. The mind must decide what belongs together, what should be separated, and what existing knowledge must be revised. The three concepts — continuity, boundary, and update — describe those operations. They are not three separate memory systems, they are three interlocking processes that allow experience to become usable memory. Continuity gives memory temporal glue. Boundary gives memory shape. Update gives memory learning value. The three operations together explain how experience is transformed from a stream into structured, revisable knowledge.

Continuity: how neighbouring moments become connected

Continuity is the process by which events that occur near one another become linked. Temporal Context Models and Context Maintenance and Retrieval models propose that memory is shaped by a slowly drifting internal context. As perception unfolds, the current moment is encoded together with traces of the recent past. This creates a gradient of association: neighbouring items or events are more likely to cue one another because they share overlapping temporal context. During recall, reinstating part of that context can help recover adjacent memories.

This explains why remembering one detail often brings back the next detail, the surrounding room, the previous conversation, or the emotional tone of the period. Memory does not only store isolated contents; it stores contents within a contextual field. The field changes gradually, which is why experience can feel continuous even though perception is made from many discrete moments. Continuity gives memory its thread.

Continuity also has a cost. If everything flows into everything else, experience becomes hard to segment. A continuous stream must be organised into units that can later be named, compared, and interpreted. This is where boundaries become necessary.

Boundary: how the stream of experience is segmented

An event boundary occurs when the current model of what is happening no longer predicts the next moment well. Changes in goal, location, actor, time, cause, or emotional significance can all mark a boundary. Event Segmentation Theory describes perception as an ongoing attempt to maintain an event model; when prediction error rises, the model is reset or revised. The result is a separation between “what was happening before” and “what is happening now.”

Boundaries are not merely subjective chapter breaks. Neuroscience evidence suggests that the brain tracks event structure during continuous experience. Studies of narrative perception show that event boundaries are reflected in changing neural activity patterns, and hippocampal responses have been associated with boundaries in continuous experience.

Boundaries help memory by creating structure. They protect one event from being confused with another, support later ordering, and make it possible to summarise experience as a sequence of episodes. Yet boundaries also change what is remembered. Information near a boundary may become especially salient, while associations across a boundary may weaken. In this sense, memory is organised by both integration and separation: continuity links moments; boundaries divide them.

Update: how experience changes the knowledge structure

Once experience has been linked and segmented, it must be interpreted. A schema is a knowledge scaffold: a structured expectation about how a situation, object, role, or sequence usually works. Schemas allow the mind to compress experience. When new information fits an existing schema, it can be encoded and consolidated more efficiently because it has a ready-made structure to attach to. Research on schemas and systems consolidation suggests that prior knowledge can accelerate the integration of congruent information.

But schemas must also remain flexible. When experience violates expectation, the mind has to decide whether the discrepancy is a minor exception, a reason to revise the schema, or evidence that a new schema is needed. Prediction error therefore has a double role: it can mark an event boundary, and it can also trigger updating. Reward prediction errors, for example, have been shown to create event boundaries in memory. This links segmentation and learning: a surprising outcome does not simply interrupt experience; it reorganises how that experience will later be remembered.

Update is the step that turns memory from storage into adaptation. A memory system that only preserved the past would be brittle. A useful memory system extracts structure from the past so it can guide future perception, action, and expectation. Schemas are the compressed results of that work.

How the three operations interact

The sequence Continuity → Boundary → Update should not be read as a one-way mechanical chain. In lived cognition, the three processes continuously influence one another. Continuity maintains the background context that makes an event coherent. Boundaries punctuate that context when the situation changes. Update then alters the schemas that will shape later continuity and boundary detection.

For example, during a conversation, continuity lets each sentence inherit meaning from the previous sentences. A sudden change of topic, tone, or speaker intention creates a boundary. If the change reveals something important — a new motive, a misunderstanding, a shift in trust — the schema for that person or situation may be updated. The next conversation will then be interpreted through that revised schema.

This is why memory is both stable and changeable. Continuity preserves relations across time; boundaries prevent experience from dissolving into an undifferentiated flow; update allows the system to learn. Together they make memory reconstructive rather than merely reproductive.

Living Memory

For a theory of living memory, these concepts are useful because they describe memory as organisation. The mind selects what belongs together, marks where one structure gives way to another, and reconstructs future meaning by revising its internal models. This fits the broader pattern of memory as a dynamic process rather than a passive archive.

The model is also practical. In writing, research, and design, continuity is created by maintaining a thread of context; boundaries are created by headings, scene shifts, conceptual breaks, or changes in visual form; update occurs when the reader’s interpretive schema changes. A strong essay, diagram, or artwork often works because it manages all three: it carries the viewer forward, marks meaningful transitions, and leaves them with a revised structure of understanding.

Glossary

  • Temporal context: A slowly drifting internal state that binds items over time and is reinstated during recall.
  • Event boundary: A reset point when prediction error increases (goal/scene/actor/time/causal change), segmenting experience.
  • Schema: An abstract knowledge scaffold that supports rapid integration of congruent information and guides prediction.
  • Prediction error: Discrepancy between expected and observed input; can induce boundaries and reorganization.
  • Arousal signature: Transient autonomic/LC‑NE responses (e.g., pupil dilation) that often accompany boundaries.
